hints: Think of entropy as a count of how many ways particles and their energy can be spread out and arranged, not just as disorder in words.
walkthrough:
Picture what entropy counts**
Imagine a solid crystal where every particle is locked in place with little energy to share, compared with a gas where particles fly everywhere. Entropy counts how many different ways you can arrange both the particles and the quanta of energy among them. More ways means higher entropy.
Final answer: Entropy is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of particles and energy in a system.

hints: Compare freedom of movement in each change: gas to liquid versus ordered solid lattice to mobile aqueous ions.
walkthrough:
Link state to freedom**
Remember the order of entropy: $\text{solid} < \text{liquid} < \text{gas}$ and $\text{aqueous ions} > \text{solid}$. A gas has huge disorder, a liquid much less, while a regular ionic lattice is very ordered compared with ions free to move in solution.

Apply to the two processes**
When steam, $\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$, condenses to $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$, particles become much more ordered so disorder falls and $\Delta S$ is negative. When solid $\text{KCl}$ breaks up into mobile $\text{K}^+\text{(aq)}$ and $\text{Cl}^-\text{(aq)}$, disorder rises so $\Delta S$ is positive.
Final answer: steam condensing into water: $\Delta S$ is negative; solid $\text{KCl}$ dissolving in water: $\Delta S$ is positive.

hints: Recall the rule for any state function from standard data: sum for products minus sum for reactants, with each $S^\circ$ multiplied by its balancing number.

Write out the expression for $2\text{ClF}_3\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2\text{(g)} + 3\text{F}_2\text{(g)}$ using $+223.1$, $+203.0$ and $+281.6$ $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$ and check the signs before evaluating.
walkthrough:
Set up the entropy balance**
For any reaction, the standard change is products minus reactants:
$$\Delta S^\circ = \Sigma nS^\circ(\text{products}) - \Sigma nS^\circ(\text{reactants})$$
Here $n$ is the balancing number. So for reaction 1:
$$\Delta S^\circ = [S^\circ(\text{Cl}_2) + 3S^\circ(\text{F}_2)] - [2S^\circ(\text{ClF}_3)]$$

Substitute and evaluate**
Put in the Table 3.2 values in $\text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$:
$$\Delta S^\circ = (223.1 + 3 \times 203.0) - (2 \times 281.6)$$
$$\Delta S^\circ = (223.1 + 609.0) - 563.2 = 832.1 - 563.2 = +268.9\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
The sign is positive, which makes sense because 2 mol of gas gives 4 mol of gas.
Final answer: $\Delta S^\circ = \Sigma S^\circ(\text{products}) - \Sigma S^\circ(\text{reactants}) = (223.1 + 3 \times 203.0) - (2 \times 281.6) = +268.9\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Look at the states in $\text{MCO}_3\text{(s)} \rightarrow \text{MO(s)} + \text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$ and think which side has the highly disordered gas.
walkthrough:
Spot the gas**
On the left you have only a solid, $\text{MCO}_3\text{(s)}$. On the right you have a solid plus $\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$. Gases carry far more ways of arranging particles and energy than solids, so forming a gas from solids always boosts disorder. That means $\Delta S$ is positive.
Final answer: $\Delta S$ is positive because a gas, $\text{CO}_2$, is produced on the right while there is no gas on the left.

hints: Rewrite $\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ$ in the form $y = mx + c$ with $y = \Delta G^\circ$ and $x = T$ to identify what gradient and intercept represent.
Pick two widely spaced points on the Fig. 3.1 line to find $\Delta G^\circ$ fall over $T$ rise, remembering to keep $\Delta G^\circ$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ for the gradient step.
Read the temperature where the line crosses $\Delta G^\circ = 0$, since feasibility starts when $\Delta G^\circ$ becomes negative.
Use the y-intercept (extrapolated to $T = 0$) or $\Delta H^\circ = \Delta G^\circ + T\Delta S^\circ$ at any point to obtain $\Delta H^\circ$ in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Turn Gibbs into $y = mx + c$**
Write the Gibbs equation with $\Delta G^\circ$ as $y$ and $T$ as $x$:
$$\Delta G^\circ = (-\Delta S^\circ)T + \Delta H^\circ$$
So a plot of $\Delta G^\circ$ against $T$ is a straight line with gradient $m = -\Delta S^\circ$ and y-intercept $c = \Delta H^\circ$. Because $\Delta S^\circ$ is positive here, the gradient is negative and the line slopes down.

Get $\Delta S^\circ$ from the gradient**
Take a large run, for example $\Delta G^\circ$ falls by about $140\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ when $T$ rises by about $900\ \text{K}$:
$$\text{gradient} = \frac{\Delta(\Delta G^\circ)}{\Delta T} \approx \frac{-140}{900} \approx -0.1556\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Since gradient $= -\Delta S^\circ$:
$$\Delta S^\circ = +0.1556\ \text{kJ K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = +0.1556 \times 1000 = +155.6\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Tolerance gives $+155.6 \pm 5\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Find the feasible temperature**
A reaction is feasible when $\Delta G^\circ \le 0$. On Fig. 3.1 that is where the line cuts the $T$ axis ($\Delta G^\circ = 0$). Reading across gives:
$$T \approx 1120 \pm 5\ \text{K}$$
Above this $T$, the $-T\Delta S^\circ$ term wins and $\Delta G^\circ$ is negative.

Get $\Delta H^\circ$ from the intercept**
The intercept at $T = 0$ is $\Delta H^\circ$. Extrapolating the line back to the $G^\circ$ axis gives about $+172\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. You can check with $\Delta H^\circ = T\Delta S^\circ$ at $\Delta G^\circ = 0$:
$$\Delta H^\circ \approx 1120 \times 0.1556 \approx 174\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
So $\Delta H^\circ = +172 \pm 10\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, positive as expected for thermal decomposition.

Final answer: $\Delta S^\circ$ for reaction 2 $= +155.6 \pm 5\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$; minimum $T = 1120 \pm 5\ \text{K}$; $\Delta H^\circ$ for reaction 2 $= +172 \pm 10\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
